blocks.text: **The task.** Given a **sorted** array and a target, find two numbers that add up to the target and return their indices. Exactly one solution exists.
The array is already sorted, so the reduction shape applies directly. Start at both ends and let the comparison steer.

blocks.code:
[2, 7, 11, 15]  target 9

left=0 right=3   2 + 15 = 17  > 9   ->  right--
left=0 right=2   2 + 11 = 13  > 9   ->  right--
left=0 right=1   2 +  7 =  9  ==     ->  found [0, 1]

blocks.text: Three iterations instead of the six pairs a nested loop would test. On a large array the gap becomes enormous.
Why it cannot miss the answer
This is the part worth convincing yourself of. Every move discards only pairs that were already impossible.

When the sum exceeds the target and we move `right` inward, we discard every pair containing that `arr[right]`. But `arr[left]` was the smallest value still available — if even the smallest partner was too big, no partner works. The discarded pairs could never have been the answer.
**Time: O(N)** — the pointers only close inward, so at most N steps.
Compare with the hash map solution to the unsorted version: also O(N) time, but O(N) space. When the input is sorted, two pointers is strictly better.
